See also Ibn Ezra, Ramban, Chizkuni, Sforno, and Ohr HaChaim who attempt to resolve the apparent inconsistencies in the verses in their seemingly interchangeable references to Ishmaelites and Midianites.
Several other authorities explain the earlier verses according to their simple meaning – that the Midianites, and not the brothers, drew Joseph from the pit and sold him to the Ishmaelites. This is the opinion of Rashbam, Chizkuni, and R’ Bachya, as well as several more recent commentators. (See Ha’amek Davar that the brothers did see the Midianites draw Joseph out and sell him to the Ishmaelites – and they were happy that the deed was done but they didn’t have to do it personally.) If so, what did Joseph mean when he revealed himself to his brothers, saying “I am Joseph … whom you sold to Egypt?” It just means that they, by casting him into the pit, began the process which resulted in his eventual sale to Egypt. Chizkuni further adds that had the brothers actually believed Joseph was still alive, as soon as they regretted their actions (which they surely did after – see Gen. 37:30 and 42:21-22), they would have undoubtedly combed the earth searching for him rather than leaving matters as they were. It’s also much more likely that they would have identified the Egyptian viceroy as Joseph had they suspected he was still alive.
(Rashbam and Chizkuni also entertain that it was in fact the brothers who sold Joseph, but they had the Midianites draw him out of the hole, as the verse implies. See similarly Da’as Zekeinim cited above.)
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: When Was the Torah Written Down?
questions.question: Exactly what was taught to Moses and Israel at Sinai, and when were the Jewish people given the Torah in the form we have it today? If Moses received the actual Torah at Sinai, didn’t it include stories which didn’t even happen yet – like the events of the Books of Numbers and Deuteronomy?

answers.text:
Thank you for raising this important issue. The Torah as we know it wasn’t given to the Jewish people at Sinai itself. Its transmission was actually a longer process which began before the Revelation at Sinai and concluded in their fortieth year in the desert. I will outline it below.
At Mount Sinai, before Moses ascended the mountain, he prepared the Jewish people for their upcoming encounter with God. Of course, the most critical prerequisite was asking the Jews if they were willing to accept the Torah. Accordingly, towards the end of the preparations, the verse states that Moses told the nation “all the words of God and all these laws,” and the Jewish people responded: “We will do” (Exodus 24:3; a few verses later they would respond more fully: “We will do and we will hear”). Moses then wrote down the information he had just imparted to the Jews. The commentator Rashi explains that the “words of God” and “all these laws” Moses wrote were: (a) the entire beginning of the Torah – i.e., the Book of Genesis and the earlier parts of the Book of Exodus, describing the bondage in Egypt and the Exodus, and (b) the laws the Jews had earlier been taught when they encamped at Marah – such as the Seven Noahide Laws, Shabbat, honoring one’s parents, and civil law. (Marah was Israel’s first encampment after the Splitting of the Sea (Exodus 15:22-26). Verse 25 there states that Moses gave the nation “statutes and laws” – i.e., some sampling of the Torah’s laws.) Thus, even before the Revelation at Sinai, the earlier parts of the Torah – namely, Genesis and the first part of Exodus – history until that time – were already written down, presumably in their current form. (See Mechilta BaChodesh 3, Sanhedrin 56b.)
Every part of the Torah which was written down was dictated directly from God to Moses (see Talmud Menachot 30a).
At Mount Sinai itself, Moses stood before the terrified yet exhilarated nation as God uttered the Ten Commandments and Moses repeated them to the nation. The first two commandments the Jews heard directly from God (see Talmud Makkot 23b-24a), while the remaining eight they witnessed God communicating to Moses, and Moses then repeated them to the nation (see Exodus 19:9, Deut. 5:4-5).
At the end of the Revelation, Moses stayed on Mount Sinai for forty days while God taught him the Torah. At the conclusion of the forty days, Moses descended with the Tablets containing the Ten Commandments. (Unfortunately, those Tablets were immediately destroyed because he came down to find a small number of people worshiping the Golden Calf and most of the nation indifferent. Moses then spent forty days praying for the Jews, and then yet another forty days studying the Torah a second time and receiving a new set of Tablets.) In any event, the Torah we have today certainly had not yet been written during or after the Sinaitic Revelation. All Moses came down with was the set of Tablets containing the Decalogue, not the entire Torah we have today.
(Of course, in one sense, the Torah preexisted the world. The Sages list the Torah as one of the entities which preceded the world’s creation (see Pesachim 54a, Bereishis Rabbah 1:4). Certainly, all the concepts and mitzvos of the Torah are eternal – Divine truths not dependent on the world’s existence. (Kabbalists explain that the Torah exists in more spiritual forms in the higher spheres of existence – where the physical mitzvos of the Torah do not apply. This too is the form in which it existed before the physical world came into being.) Similarly, the Ramban (Nachmanides; Intro. to the Torah) explains that while the Torah was still in Heaven, before it was given to Moses, it existed as an unbroken sequence of letters, not yet divided into distinct words. Thus, the Torah’s wisdom did exist in some form before it was brought down from Heaven. The question we are dealing with is when it was given to man, assuming the form it has today.)
What exactly did Moses study for the forty days he stood on Mount Sinai? It is a debate in the Talmud (Hagigah 6a-b and elsewhere). One opinion was that he studied the Torah in all its details, while another was that he studied the Torah’s general principles, while the details he learned from God later, in the Tent of Meeting, during Israel’s forty years in the desert. (Everyone would appear to agree that every last detail of the Torah had not been taught at Sinai. There were laws which came up in the desert that Moses himself did not know – such as that one who is unable to bring the Paschal Lamb on Passover can offer it a month later (on Pesach Sheni), and that if a man has no sons, his daughter inherits his property. See Numbers 9:6-12; 27:1-11)
When was the Torah recorded in writing? That too is a debate (Talmud Gittin 60a). R’ Yochanan maintains that the Torah was written one section at a time during Israel’s forty years in the desert, each section added as it was studied (and as new events occurred). Reish Lakish holds that the Torah was written down only when it was entirely complete at the end of Israel’s sojourn in the desert. Regardless, it was surely completed in Moses’s lifetime, as the Torah itself records that Moses gave the Torah scroll to his tribe (Levi) for safekeeping (Deut. 31:9,24-26).
One final issue remains. The final eight verses of the Torah describe Moses’s death and burial. There is obviously no way Moses could have written those after they occurred! The Talmud debates this as well (Bava Batra 15a, Menachot 30a). R’ Yehuda understands that God dictated them to Moses’s disciple Joshua, who transcribed them, while R’ Shimon maintains that Moses himself wrote the account of his death – “with tears.”
See here for more information on the account of the Torah’s writing and transmission.
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: Hidden Light (Ohr HaGanuz) of Creation
questions.question: If God created light on the first day of creation, what is the idea that He created the heavenly bodies on the fourth? Where was the light coming from beforehand if not from the sun and stars?

answers.text:
Thank you for raising your interesting issue. The Talmud (Hagigah 12a) asks your exact question and gives two answers. The simpler answer is that God did in fact create the heavenly bodies on the first day, with His creation of the light. However, He did not yet arrange them in their respective places until the fourth day. In fact, the Midrash states that all the elements of creation were created on the first day of creation. Each was then put in its place within the earth or the cosmos on the appropriate day of creation (Bereishis Rabbah 1:19; see Rashi to Genesis 1:14,24).
The second answer given by the Talmud is that the light of the first day was not the light of the sun but a much greater and loftier creation – the original, unfiltered Light of Creation. With it, a person could see from one end of the world to the other. However, God foresaw that the world would eventually contain wicked people who were not worthy of enjoying such esoteric light. He therefore hid it away for the righteous in the World to Come.
We call this original Light of Creation the “Hidden Light” (ohr ha’ganuz) – as it was hidden away for the future. As is clear from the Talmud, it is not ordinary light but a spiritual essence too lofty for the physical world. It was the first entity God created outside Himself – with His very first utterance of “Let there be light.” This light is thus the part of creation which is so to speak “closest” to God – the most spiritual of all His creations (see The Science of God by Prof. Gerald Schroeder, pp. 161-165). Only the righteous in the World to Come will be able to bask in its glow. (The Sages state that this light was not hidden until after the first Shabbat of Creation (see Rashi to Bereishis 1:14).)
There is an interesting allusion to the existence of the Hidden Light in the wording of the Torah itself. The first light God created is called ohr, meaning “light”. By contrast, the verses discussing the fourth day of creation (Genesis 1:14-19) describe how God created the “me’orot” – which literally translates “from lights.” In other words, the heavenly bodies are not true light, but “from lights” – distant reflections of the true heavenly Light of Creation. They are energized by God’s true light, but they are covered and obscured by layers of physicality on the outside – so that they reflect God’s original light in highly attenuated form – enabling man to benefit from God’s illumination without being destroyed by its true inner radiance.
A deeper way of understanding the Original Light is as follows. We quoted above the Talmud’s statement that using the Hidden Light a person can see from one end of the world to the other. The idea is not that this light is physically brighter than today’s light. It is rather that it is so radiant and spiritually charged that it reveals reality as it actually is. It creates pure and unadulterated awareness – of everything in creation. It is the light of revelation – of shining God’s truth upon the world, revealing reality as it actually is and not as we finite beings perceive it.
Today, without this light, the truth is often hidden and God’s presence is badly obscured. We cannot even tell right from wrong. But the Original Light, a creation so holy and close to God, shines with complete and absolute clarity, leaving no room for falsehood or self-delusion. Today a person can act wickedly and either ignore it or somehow pretend his actions are justified. We can live with ourselves despite our flaws, almost pretending God isn’t really paying attention to us – since in our world of limited, physical light, we do not actually see God. However, in the Future World, with the true Light of Creation shining, there will be complete clarity – and knowledge of God. We will not be able to ignore or hide our faults. We will see our goodness and wickedness before us with complete lucidity.
The Talmud (Avodah Zarah 3b) writes as follows (slightly paraphrased): “In the End of Days, there will no longer be Gehenna. Rather, the Holy One, blessed be He, will take the sun out of its sheath and it will pierce. The wicked will be judged through it and the righteous will be healed through it.” Based on what we have explained, the meaning is that in the future, God will remove the covering from the true Light of Creation. (Recall that the heavenly bodies are referred to as “from lights.” They have the Light of Creation within them, but obscure it in layers of physicality. In the future, God will remove the “cover” from the sun – revealing His true light.) This intense light will bring complete clarity to the universe. The wicked will realize they have sinned and that absolute knowledge, with no way to hide from it, will destroy them entirely. Conversely, the righteous will now know just how good and worthy they were, and they will bask in their true and total knowledge of their closeness to God (as heard from R’ Yochanan Zweig).
(Some explain the Plague of Darkness in Egypt in a similar vein. The Sages tell us that while it was dark for the Egyptians, the Jews were bathed in light – and could even see where their Egyptians kept their valuables (Shemos Rabbah 14:3; Rashi to Shemos 10:23). Quite possibly, what God did was reveal His true light – at least to some small degree. This engulfed the wicked Egyptians, who couldn’t handle such unfiltered truth, in total darkness, while the worthier Jews benefited from this lofty light and could see piercingly – even discovering where the Egyptians placed their hidden treasures.)
(See Afikei Yam to Talmud Bava Metziah 86b, Nedarim 8b and Avodah Zarah 3a.)
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: Jews Owning Property in Egypt
questions.question: How did the Israelites own so much cattle when they departed Egypt? Weren’t they slaves who basically owned nothing of their own?

answers.text:
It’s actually interesting. Although we were slaves in Egypt, it does seem that we were allowed to own our own personal property – especially livestock. The Jewish people originally descended to Egypt in Joseph’s time as pastoralists, coming with large herds of sheep and cattle (which lacked grazing land in Canaan due to the famine; see Genesis 46:31-47:6). And despite their later enslavement, we never find that the Egyptians confiscated the Israelites’ property. Thus, at the end of the slavery, we had no difficulty offering a sheep or goat for the Paschal offering. The Torah further attests that when we departed Egypt, we left with huge flocks of animals (Exodus 12:38). Lastly, when the Plague of Pestilence occurred, striking all the Egyptian livestock (which weren’t brought indoors – see Rashi to Exodus 9:10), Moses emphasized that not a single Jewish animal would die – and that is indeed what occurred (Exodus 9:1-7).
Another indication that the Jews were able to own money was when Pharaoh’s daughter gave the baby she found, whom she would later name Moses, to his mother to nurse. She promised his mother, Yocheved, that she would pay her for her services (Exodus 2:9). Thus, apparently, Jews were able to earn money on the side – perhaps even enough to save up and purchase their freedom. (In truth, Yocheved was from the Tribe of Levi, which according to the Midrash was exempt from the bondage (Shemos Rabbah 5:16). However, Pharaoh’s daughter certainly didn’t know the baby’s tribe (just saying, “from the children of the Hebrews is this”). Thus clearly, offering to pay a Jewish wet-nurse for her services was appropriate behavior during the servitude.)
It should furthermore be kept in mind that for the most part, the Jews were not slaves to individual Egyptians. We were rather slaves directly to Pharaoh (Rashi to Exodus 20:2, citing Mechilta), i.e., his personal workforce. Thus, despite the torturous slavery we were subject to in Egypt, we did have a certain status as the king’s royal servants - not lowly slaves to every commoner in Egypt. Perhaps that granted us more privileges, including property rights.
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: Rachel’s Tomb (Kever Rochel) Today
questions.question: The Torah states that Jacob put up a monument on Rachel’s grave which stands till today (Genesis 35:20). Does that refer to the domed building which has always stood over her grave?

answers.text:
Actually, no. In general, when the Torah states “until today,” it refers to Moses’s time, when the Torah as we have it was first written down (Radak; see Talmud Yoma 54a). (Some alternatively explain that “until today” alludes to the fact that the location of her grave would never be forgotten or that it will eternally be a place of worship and pilgrimage for Jews.) There is a longstanding tradition that Rachel’s grave really is where we believe it is today – as the location has been revered by Jews, Christians, and Muslims throughout the ages. But whatever monument Jacob stood up there is surely long lost.
Incidentally, Jacob’s placement of a monument over Rachel’s grave is the earliest source of the universal Jewish custom of placing a headstone over a grave. In Hebrew it is called a matzeiva, from the root word yatzav – standing straight and erect – just as a matzeiva is vertically placed at the head of the grave. Some explain that this custom alludes to our belief that ultimately, the dead will stand up again – when they return to life at the Resurrection.
In terms of the building over Rachel’s tomb, it is definitely old but nowhere near Biblically old. Many structures have stood over the tomb over the millennia – as attested to by travelers throughout the ages, going as far back as the 4th century. The domed structure we are familiar with today is believed to have been constructed by Muslims in the 15th century. In 1841 and 1845, Sir Moses Montefiore financed its restoration and expansion, adding an antechamber before the domed area.
Up until 1948, Rachel’s Tomb was in an open area on the roadside, with a Muslim cemetery added alongside it. During the years from 1948-1967, under Jordanian control, Bethlehem expanded beyond the area of the tomb. From 1967, it again became a place of pilgrimage for Jews, who would enter the city of Bethlehem to reach it. However, once the Intifadas began, especially the Second Intifada of 2000, the location became dangerous for Jews, effectively excluding them from visiting it. One time in 2001, an attack trapped fifty Jews inside the building until the Israeli army was able to extricate them. But afterwards, Israel slightly extended the barrier between Israel and the West Bank in order to place Rachel’s Tomb on the Israeli side, and it subsequently safeguarded the area with further concrete barriers. Thus, it is a secure place to visit today, although its famous domed structure from over the centuries is hardly unrecognizable.
Rachel’s Tomb is one of the world’s most auspicious places for prayer. Jeremiah himself, considered one of the sterner prophets, describes how Mother Rachel cried out for her exiled children, and God heeded her cries, promising that the Jews would return to their land (Jeremiah 31:14-16). The Sages even more poignantly depict Rachel as coming out of her grave to stand alongside the Jews as they were on their way to the Babylonian Exile, beseeching God to have mercy on them (Midrash, cited in Rashi to Bereishis 48:7). My wife says that she personally finds Kever Rachel more deeply moving than the Western Wall itself. Further, since Rachel herself was barren for the first seven years of her marriage, until she was blessed with Joseph, her grave is considered an especially appropriate place to pray for children.
One final aspect of Rachel’s Tomb bears mention. On September 9, 2003, a Palestinian suicide bomber blew himself up outside Café Hillel in the German Colony in Jerusalem. It killed seven people and wounded fifty. Among the slain were Rabbi Dr. David Applebaum, chief physician of emergency care at Shaarei Tzedek Hospital, and his 20-year-old daughter Nava, who had gone out together the night before her wedding, murdering her on the eve of the new life she never lived to see. A part of her unused wedding gown was made into a covering for the ark at Rachel’s Tomb. It bears the inscription: “Nava Applebaum, a Bride for Eternity.” We can thus hardly imagine how much heartbreak and how many tears combine with the prayers of those who come to pray at Rachel’s Tomb today, surely transporting their prayers directly to Heaven.
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: Was Megillat Esther a Religious Book?
questions.question: I read a post by a non-Orthodox Rabbi who claimed that Megillat Esther is really a secular work. Not only is God’s name never mentioned, but there is almost no mention of Jewish life or practice in the Megillah. Some examples he gave were the fact that the Jews participated in Ahasuerus’s feast, seemingly indifferent to the fact that they were eating non-kosher food and drinking Gentile wine. Even after the decree we don’t find Mordechai and other Jews praying or gathering in their synagogues (if they had any), only wearing sackcloth and ashes. Esther likewise has the residents of Shushan fast for three days but never seems to pray to God. Even after the victory, the Megillah writes that the Jews celebrated but didn’t seem to offer prayers of thanksgiving. How would you respond to this?

answers.text:
In one sense it is true that the Jewish people as a whole did not seem to be particularly religious during the Purim story. They had already spread entirely throughout Ahasuerus’s huge empire in a relatively short time – in a span of about two generations – no doubt in search of commerce and wealth, and seemingly with little concern for religious life and community. The Jews had apparently assimilated fairly quickly. And the writer is correct that their willingness to attend Ahasuerus’s non-kosher feast also paints an image of a people which gave higher priority to their acceptance by the Gentiles than their religious observance.
However, in spite of that backdrop, Megillat Esther is actually a very spiritual book – describing how Mordechai and Esther heroically stemmed the Jewish people’s assimilative tendencies and led them to a strengthened Jewish identity and repentance – a repentance which averted Haman’s decree and brought about the Purim salvation. It’s fairly easy to see this in the storyline itself, even without the much more profound interpretations of the Talmud and Midrash – which are many. Here are a few key points which most strongly highlight this:
(1) Mordechai refused to bow down to Haman (Esther 3:2). This was clearly religiously motivated.
(2) Haman, when he went to convince the king to annihilate the Jews, pointed out that their laws are different from the laws of all other peoples (3:8). So clearly, the Jewish people as a whole were somewhat observant, provoking Haman’s anger.
(3) When Haman’s decree is publicized, the Jews all turn to mourning, fasting, and crying, wearing sackcloth and ashes (4:3). Although the word prayer does not explicitly appear, these are clearly acts of penitence. Obviously, such acts were directed toward God, since for a secular person, they would serve absolutely no purpose.
(4) Esther sees that Mordechai is publicly mourning and cannot enter the palace compound in sackcloth. She sends him nicer clothes to enable him to enter but he refuses to accept them (4:4). Now if Mordechai wanted to avert the decree through practical means, he would have contacted Esther at once. But he recognized that the only way to save the Jews was through turning to God – even at the expense of being able to reach the Queen.
(5) Esther likewise decrees a three-day fast (4:16) – surely another act of repentance. In fact, the commentators explain that this atoned for their participation in Ahasuerus’s forbidden feast.
(6) At the end of the story, Mordechai and Esther instituted Purim as a religious holiday to be observed for all generations. The Jews accepted it as they accepted the fast days they were already observing (see espec. end of Ch. 9).
It is thus clear that Megillat Esther is at its heart a very spiritual story. The Jews were lax, they were threatened with extermination, and they repented – averting the decree against them. And they lastly eternally commemorated the salvation with a new Jewish holiday.
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: Leaving the House on Shabbat
questions.question: After the Exodus, when the Israelites were in the desert, some of them wrongly went out on Shabbat to search of manna. In response, God told Moses “Let every man remain in his place; let no man leave his place on the seventh day” (Exodus 16:29). Why do Jews not observe this today? How can we go to synagogue or take a walk on Shabbat if the Torah writes explicitly that we may not leave our homes?

answers.text:
Thank you for your interesting question. The verse doesn’t exactly say a person shouldn’t leave his home but that he shouldn’t leave his “place”. What exactly is a person’s “place”?
Looking carefully at that verse, it contains two phrases. To understand it properly, we need to examine the implications of each one. I’ll do that very briefly below:
“Let every man remain in his place:” The Hebrew terms the Torah uses for “place” here is “tachtav” – literally, “beneath him.” This implies a person may not move from his position at all. Now, the tradition of our Sages is that there is no obligation that we remain frozen in our places the entire Shabbat. Even with the Rabbinical restrictions of this law, we may walk throughout our entire city and up to 2000 cubits (around 3000 feet) beyond the city limits in every direction. Thus, explain the Sages, our verse’s restriction that we stay in our place refers to a person who has improperly gone beyond the 2000-cubit limit of his permitted travels. Such a person must stay put for the remainder of Shabbat (Talmud Eiruvin 51a; Mechilta, Vayisa 5). (He actually can go 4 cubits in any direction – the area considered his “place”. Note also that since most Jews live in large metropolitan areas, our cities extend almost indefinitely and this restriction is rarely relevant.)
“Let no man leave his place on the seventh day:” Here the Torah uses the word “makom” to refer to a person’s place. Makom is a more generic word, not necessarily referring to a person’s precise location. Accordingly, the Sages understand that this refers to the law that we may not leave our general location on Shabbat. According to some opinions, this means that a person may not travel more than 12 mil = 24,000 cubits in any direction on Shabbat. (See Eiruvin 17b. The Rabbis extended this prohibition to forbid going even 2000 cubits outside our city or location on Shabbat.) Others explain that the entire law forbidding travel on Shabbat is Rabbinical to begin with. Thus, our verse is only seen as an allusion to the 2000 cubits the Sages would later forbid (Mechilta there).
I have read that the early Karaites insisted that this verse means that a person may not leave his home the entire Shabbat – but eventually (and for obvious reasons) they came to accept the tradition of the Sages.
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: What Was Sinful About Building the Tower of Babel?
questions.question: I’ve often wondered what the builders of the Tower of Babel did to deserve the punishment they received. All the Torah says is that they decided to build a city with a tall tower reaching the sky. And their stated reason for doing so was so that they’ll make a name for themselves and not be scattered throughout the world. What actually was wrong with that? The people seemed to all be at peace with each other. And even though they intended to have their tower reach heaven, they obviously couldn’t really reach God’s domain with a tall tower alone! It’s not likely they could have built a structure as high as our steel-and-concrete skyscrapers of today – certainly not our satellites and rockets. And I don’t think we’re being punished for building those!

answers.text:
Thank you for your incisive question. You are right that on the surface the builders of the Tower did not seem to have any very wicked motives in mind. Yet it is clear that God discerned in them some very negative intentions deserving severe punishment. They were clearly using their unity for some terribly nefarious purpose – although the Torah does not spell out for us precisely what it was.
The Talmud (Sanhedrin 109a) explains that the intention of the builders was not just to reach up to Heaven but to invade it – refusing to be relegated to a lower domain than God. They wanted to take God on directly in Heaven – as ridiculous as that sounds to us. In fact, according to the Sages, their leader Nimrod would later throw Abraham into a furnace (from which he was saved) in attempt to stamp out the belief in God he was beginning to disseminate. (See Talmud Hullin 89a, Eiruvin 53a, Bereishis Rabbah 38:13.)
The Talmud divides the builders into three categories: (a) Those who wanted to reach Heavens to literally fight against God. (b) Those who wanted to go to Heaven to live - complaining that God has no right to choose the Heavens for Himself. (c) Those who wanted to ascend to Heaven in order to worship idols. The Midrash (Bereishis Rabbah 38:6) similarly explains that they were going to place an idol on top of their tower with a sword in its hand as if in battle with God. (In this sense, their Tower resembled the ziggurats of ancient Mesopotamia (the probable location of the Tower of Babel) – a manmade tower to heaven atop which an imagined deity resided. Perhaps, following the Talmud that the builders actually wanted to ascend to Heaven, they wanted to bring their idol with them in order to give it equal standing with God.)
Another opinion, which appears in the Midrash (ibid.), is that the builders of the Tower wanted to avoid suffering any future worldwide floods. They thought their huge tower could serve as one of a set of pillars supporting the Heavens and keeping them from “shaking” and spilling out so much rain. Apart from their rather primitive understanding of meteorology, clearly such people refused to accept the actual message of the Flood – that it was an act of God punishing the wicked for their sins. They insisted on seeing it as a periodic naturally-occurring event – which they could avoid through taking the proper precautions. And God judged them extremely harshly for this. Indeed, according to the Sages, this occurred in Noah’s lifetime – when the memory of the Flood was not that distant and its lesson should have still reverberated.
In any event, the fact that the builders could not possibly have actually reached Heaven was irrelevant. It was their evil intent which God noted – and judged. In fact, the Talmud also writes that apart from the punishments the builders of the Tower received in this world, none of them received a share in the World to Come (Sanhedrin 107b).
Other commentators take a more literal interpretation of this episode – not that the builders of the Tower literally wanted to rebel against God, but that they wanted to create an extremely powerful empire, granting them fame or world domination – no doubt wanting mankind to pay homage to them rather than God. (See Bechor Shor, Radak, Chizkuni, R. Hirsch.) Alternatively, they wanted to all live together – contrary to God’s plan that they spread out and populate the entire earth (R. Bachya).
You pointed out that the builders of the Tower did appear to have one positive quality in their favor: they all did seem to get along. This is a good point. The Sages note this as well (Bereishis Rabbah 38:6). In fact, they contrast the generation of the Tower to the generation of the Flood which was characterized by lawlessness and robbery (Genesis 6:1-2,11). As a result, unlike the generation of the Flood which was destroyed entirely, the generation of the Tower was merely dispersed. Peace and unity among men, even for bad purpose, is appreciated by God, and that did ameliorate their judgment. They might not have earned a share in the World to Come themselves, but they had many descendants who no doubt did.
This leads us to a final interesting observation made by my teacher Rabbi Yochanan Zweig. The one good quality of that generation was the unity they had between them – which God indeed appreciated. Yet God’s punishment was to alter their languages and separate them – taking away the one good quality they had!
R. Zweig answers that true unity is not achieved when everyone tries to be the same and live under the same roof. Each nation does in fact have a different nature and different set of skills and talents. By separating them and granting each its own unique language, each nation would be able to properly develop its own national identity. Then the nations could live together in true harmony, each preserving its particular nature while contributing its talents to the welfare of all mankind. But had they attempted to all live together as a single unit, no nation would have had the opportunity for healthy self-expression. Each nation would have been subdued before the whole and failed to develop itself. Thus, since God did in fact admire the unity the nations wanted to achieve, He divided them and gave them each their own space and language – enabling them to truly live in peace.
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: What Was Rahab's Profession?
questions.question: Was Rahab, the woman in Jericho who hid the spies Joshua sent to the land, a prostitute or an innkeeper?

answers.text:
The simple reading of the Book of Joshua (2:1) is that Rahab was a harlot (“zonah”). This is the understanding of the Talmud (Zevachim 116b), and followed by some of the commentators. Some of the commentators understand that she was an innkeeper who provided food and lodging – which would explain why the spies naturally came to her for lodging. (See Targum Yonasan who interprets literally “a seller of food;” see also Rashi and Radak.) Others explain further that very possibly she both held both “professions” (since there is clearly overlap between the two) (Abarbanel). Some further suggest that the spies came to such a person because Rahab was likely to possess wide knowledge of the goings-on and attitudes of the people.
It is significant to note in spite of Rahab’s possibly very lowly profession, she nevertheless quite heroically saved the spies – sparing herself and her family in the process (see Joshua 2). In fact, the Talmud has a tradition that she afterwards converted (at the age of 50), praying that her act of saving the spies should atone for her earlier life (Zevachim 116b). Another tradition states that she subsequently married Joshua and merited righteous descendants (Megillah 14b). Clearly, a part of the message is that regardless of our origins or even shameful history, greatness is available to anyone who will rise to the challenge.
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: Metzora – Blood Placed on Body Parts
questions.question: I was studying Leviticus chapter 14 and was wondering about the significance of the blood and oil the Kohen places on the metzora’s (leper’s) right ear, right thumb, and right big toe. What is the significance of those three places?

answers.text:
Thank you for raising your interesting issue. Ibn Ezra (14:14), a medieval Spanish commentator, explains that a person is stricken with tzara'at (often translated as leprosy) in response to his sinful behavior. The act of placing blood and oil on him alludes to the repentance demanded of him. His ear represents that he did not listen to God. The thumb is the strongest finger and the big toe the strongest toe – and for most people, their right side is their stronger side. Thus, the overall message of these applications is that the person must employ all his strength to train himself to improve.
Rav Samson Raphael Hirsch (as understood by ArtScroll Vayikra) explains similarly that the message of these three limbs is that the person must improve himself on the level of his mind (ear), his actions (thumb), and his efforts (as the big toe alludes to his forward movements). Or as I’ve seen contemporaries put it, the ear represents that the sinner refused to listen to God, his hand represents his sinful actions, and his foot signifies that he followed along a wicked path. All these limbs require atonement and so receive the sacred blood and oil.
For a deeper approach, see this article. See also the following past responses about the ailment of tzara'at:
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: Where Does the Midrash Come from?
questions.question: It has always bothered me where the Midrash comes from. Who authored it and what makes it authentic? I sometimes hear of stories and parables from the Midrash which seem far-fetched and I can’t believe could literally be true. Are such things a part of our Torah or just wild tales?

answers.text:
Thank you for raising your important issue. Before I begin addressing your question, I should point out that there are two very different bodies of literature which are both referred to as the Midrash. (The word “midrash” comes from the root “darash” – which literally means to seek or inquire. In this context, it refers to the practice of analyzing the Torah’s precise wording and deriving further meanings and inferences from it, sometimes homiletical.)
The first body of Midrashic works consists of the halachic Midrashim (e.g., Mechilta, Sifra, Sifri). These deal with the legalistic parts of the Torah, generally discussing the precise meaning of the Torah’s verses in Jewish law. Such works are in essence similar to the Mishna and Talmud and do not seem to be the subject of your question. (The main difference between the Midrash and the Talmud is that the Midrash is organized according to the verses of the Torah while the Talmud is organized logically.)
There is also an extensive body of Midrashic works which is Aggadic – dealing with non-legalistic issues – aspects of the Torah not directly impacting on Jewish law. It primarily consists of elaborations on the stories of the Torah, ethical lessons, and parables. Often, the Midrash speaks in wild metaphor – in manners clearly not intended to be taken literally – yet which teaches deeper or even Kabbalistic messages. These include such classic works as the Midrash Rabbah and Midrash Tanchuma.
In terms of its origin, in essence the Midrash comes from Sinai. It is a part of the Oral Torah taught to Moses at Sinai – as the Mishna and Talmud – but not recorded in writing until much later. (As always, the Oral Torah is a combination of actual teachings passed from Sinai and extrapolations made by later scholars, based on the accepted techniques for interpreting and making derivations in the Torah.) Thus, unlike the written Torah, which was written down word-for-word shortly after the Revelation at Sinai, the Midrash consists of teachings and lessons which were preserved in a much more living, dynamic form, and only later assumed the set form it has today. It therefore does not consist of the actual words Moses was taught at Sinai, but it contains the same messages and content. This is why the Midrash will often teach lessons using metaphors suited to the times and places of the scholars of the Talmud. They were the ones who expressed the ideas of the Midrash as we have them today, employing language and intellectual constructs contemporary to their times.
Although such Midrashic works are not legalistic and seem much less rigorous and substantial than the legal parts of the Oral Torah, they too are equally a part of our tradition. Of course, as we mentioned, such Midrashim are often not meant to be taken literally (see here for a further discussion). Yet at the same time, their lessons and messages are very much a part of our eternal Torah.
Pirkei Avot is a section of the Mishna which deals almost exclusively with ethics – not with the laws and customs which are almost the exclusive focus of the entire rest of the Mishna. It begins: “Moses received the Torah from Sinai and transmitted it to Joshua…” Pirkei Avot there provides a brief outline of the Torah’s transmission from Sinai until the early period of the Mishna. One of the commentators to the Misha, Rav Ovadiah of Bartenura (Bertinoro), asks why such an introduction – tracing the Torah back to Sinai – appears at the beginning of Pirkei Avot and not at the beginning of the entire Mishna?
He answers that it is obvious and need not be stated that the legalistic parts of the Oral Law are from Sinai. They are simply the interpretations which accompanied the Written Torah, filling in the many details not recorded in the Torah itself but which clearly must have been given at Sinai. However, the ethical advice of Pirkei Avot does not really seem like “solid” Torah. It seems no more than sage advice – surely coming from great people, but not qualitatively different from what one might read in the writings of Ben Franklin or Dale Carnegie.
This is why Pirkei Avot expressly begins with an accounting of the Torah’s transmission – to emphasize that the advice and introspections of the Sages are not just the wise musings of ancient scholars – surely less relevant and practical than contemporaries such as Jordan Peterson or Tony Robbins. Such ethics are a part of our tradition – whose origins stem directly from Sinai. Again, not every story in the Midrash is meant to be taken literally, but it must all be taken seriously – and revered to the same degree as every other part of our Torah.
It should be noted that there are in fact a very wide range of Midrashic works. Some of the classic ones – like the Midrash Rabbah and Tanchuma – are very old and considered fully authentic. (I should add that even those works were generally not compiled in their present form until much later, often well into medieval times. But they are essentially collections of much older material (as seen from the fact that they consistently quote from Talmudic sages), just put into their current forms much later. In fact, what we call the Midrash Tanchuma today is actually a combination of two or three separate Midrashic works, one of which was the original Tanchuma.) Other Midrashic works have origins much less well-known, and in fact some are of more questionable authenticity. But the main ones you will generally see cited are all considered thoroughly authentic and reliable.
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: How Could King David Take Avishag?
questions.question: I’m having a difficult time understanding the episode of King David and Avishag the Shunamite. When he was old, his servants found a young virgin to lie with him and keep him warm (I Kings 1:1-4). How was this permitted? And why couldn’t he just take one of his existing wives or marry Avishag?

answers.text:
Thank you for the good question. In those days the belief was that a virgin girl produced more warmth than a married woman, and this was considered a medical necessity for the ailing king – as nothing else was effective in keeping him warm. The commentator Malbim also suggests that they didn’t want one of his wives to be so close to him because marital relations would have further weakened him. Also, David didn't marry Avishag, not only because he was likely too old to consummate the marriage, but because he had already married the maximum number of wives permitted to a king – 18 (see Talmud Sanhedrin 21a). In addition, since divorce is so serious in the eyes of the Torah, he did not divorce one of his other wives before she came to serve him. The Sages in fact derive from here that it’s better for a man to be in seclusion with a single woman (a Rabbinical prohibition only first forbidden in King David’s time) than divorce his wife (ibid., 22a). (This obviously should not be taken as practical advice. David needed this for a serious medical condition.) Some alternatively suggest that Avishag became the king’s concubine, as kings were accustomed to have in Biblical times. Avishag was thus permitted to David, but as the verse attests, he was old and did not “know” her.
(It should be noted that King David was only 70 at this time. The commentators discuss why despite his great righteousness David aged relatively young and lived a relatively brief life.)
(Sources: Talmud Sanhedrin 21a, 22a; Radbaz IV 225: She'eilat Ya'avetz II 15.)
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: The Altalena: The Ship that Almost Started a Civil War
questions.question: The Altalena: The Ship that Almost Started a Civil War

answers.text:
Israel’s Heritage Ministry’s recent announcement of the discovery of the sunk ship Altalena is bringing to light one of the darkest moments in Israel’s early history.
Shortly after Israel declared independence in May 1948, it came dangerously close to a civil war.
The conflict culminated in the Altalena affair in June 1948, when the Israeli army, under the orders of Israel’s provisional government, attacked a military ship sent by a rival Zionist organization1. Nineteen people were killed in what the eyewitnesses described as “Jews shooting Jews.”
This tragic story had its roots in the early disagreement among Zionists on how to achieve security for Jews in the Land of Israel. After World War I, the British took control of the Land of Israel under the mandate of facilitating the creation of “a national home for the Jewish people,” as per the Balfour Declaration of 1917. However, the British did not anticipate the violent reaction of the Arab world to the idea of Jewish independence. Fueled by religious incitement, Arab mobs perpetrated massacres on the centuries-old Jewish communities in the Land of Israel. The British did nothing to protect the Jews.
Frustrated by British inaction, early Zionist leaders formed Jewish defense groups. Soon, a disagreement emerged. The first such group, Haganah, advocated restraint. Though ready to defend the Jewish community, they generally cooperated with the British authorities and did not go on the offensive.
Some felt that the policy of restraint was not enough. Among them was Ze’ev Jabotinsky, who formulated a “revisionist” version of Zionism, revising the original Zionist principles to include the use of force when necessary.
The Revisionist Zionists formed the Irgun, also known by its Hebrew acronym Etzel, a paramilitary organization willing to go on the offensive and retaliate for Arab attacks in the hopes of preventing future attacks.
Haganah member in training. Picture taken between 1944 and 1946. ארכיון גן-שמואל, CC BY 2.5 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.5>, via Wikimedia Commons
Unable to control the violence in Mandatory Palestine, the British appointed a commission of inquiry, headed by Lord Robert Peel, to investigate the situation. In 1937, the Peel committee presented its recommendations: to partition the land into two states, Jewish and Arab, and to limit Jewish immigration.
In 1939, the British government issued the infamous White Paper, setting a limit on Jewish immigration to 75,000 people over the course of five years. This limit frustrated both the original and the Revisionist Zionists, who understood that with Hitler setting out to conquer the world, Jews remaining in Europe were in great danger. While the Haganah, now under the leadership of David Ben Gurion, still held out hope for diplomacy, the Irgun redirected its military efforts from the Arabs to the British. Irgun members began bombing British military bases and killing British army officers.
In 1942, Menachem Begin, the only survivor from his immediate family in Poland, arrived in Mandatory Palestine. With his previous experience in Jabotinsky’s organization, Begin was appointed head of the Irgun in 1943.
Having witnessed the destruction of European Jewry, Begin was determined to do everything in his power to help the remaining European Jews escape the Nazis and reach the Land of Israel. The main obstacle, in his eyes, was the British government that, fully aware of the Holocaust, still insisted on enforcing the ridiculously insufficient immigration quotas.
Both the Haganah and the Irgun were involved in Aliyah Bet, the illegal smuggling of Jews into the Land of Israel. However, only a fraction of Jewish refugees made it safely to shore. Some drowned during the smuggling attempt, and others were caught by the British and sent either to detention camps or, worse, right back into the Nazis’ hands.
In February 1944, Begin issued a Declaration of Revolt, openly calling for the overthrow of British rule. The posters plastered all over the Land of Israel stated2:
[W]e face an historic decision on our future destiny… the British administration of Eretz Israel… is betraying our brethren to Hitler. Our nation will fight this regime … And this is our demand: Rule over Eretz Israel must immediately be handed over to a provisional Hebrew government… [which will:] a. establish a national Hebrew army. b. conduct negotiations with all authorized bodies on the organization of the mass evacuation of European Jewry to Eretz Israel. [T]his is the sole way of rescuing our people…
[W]e face an historic decision on our future destiny… the British administration of Eretz Israel… is betraying our brethren to Hitler. Our nation will fight this regime …
And this is our demand: Rule over Eretz Israel must immediately be handed over to a provisional Hebrew government… [which will:] a. establish a national Hebrew army. b. conduct negotiations with all authorized bodies on the organization of the mass evacuation of European Jewry to Eretz Israel.
The posters came to the attention of the British authorities, who immediately declared Begin the most wanted man. Begin went undercover, directing the Irgun from his hiding places. The revolt began with attacks on the British immigration offices and moved on to the intelligence and police headquarters.
Young David Ben-Gurion. Author unknown. CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
Ben-Gurion and other leaders of the Jewish Agency, the main body representing the Jews of the Land of Israel in the diplomatic arena, condemned the revolt.
Ben-Gurion remained steadfastly convinced that cooperation with the British government would be more effective and cost fewer Jewish lives. It would also build international support that would be necessary for Jewish statehood once the war in Europe ended. He wanted to persuade the British – and other Western governments – that Palestinian Jews, unlike their Arab neighbors, were “a civilized community and a reliable ally.”
Ben-Gurion remained steadfastly convinced that cooperation with the British government would be more effective and cost fewer Jewish lives. It would also build international support that would be necessary for Jewish statehood once the war in Europe ended. He wanted to persuade the British – and other Western governments – that Palestinian Jews, unlike their Arab neighbors, were “a civilized community and a reliable ally.”
Ben-Gurion attempted to negotiate with Begin. In October, Moshe Sneh, a Haganah commander and member of the Jewish Agency, spent five hours trying to convince Begin of the importance of international support for Zionism and the dangers of alienating the British government. Unconvinced, Begin insisted on waging a war against the British. At their next meeting, Jewish Agency representatives threatened to end Irgun operations “at all costs4.”
Concerned about the explicit threat, some Irgun members urged Begin to take action against the Jewish Agency. Begin responded, “I will never lend a hand to a war of brothers5.” Milchemet achim, literally “war of brothers,” the Hebrew term for civil war, remained out of the question for Begin for the rest of his life, even when it came to the difficult test of Altalena.
The nadir in the relations between the Jewish Agency and the Irgun was the assassination of Cairo-based Lord Moyne, who was responsible for implementing the White Paper quotas and, consequently, for deporting the hapless immigrants. Ironically, the Irgun was not involved in his assassination, which was perpetrated by Lechi, a more militant Jewish faction.
The assassination outraged the British far beyond Mandatory Palestine. Even Churchill himself issued a warning against “a new set of gangsters worthy of Nazi Germany6.”
The Jewish Agency immediately condemned the assassination. Their official statement proclaimed7, “The perpetrators of terror [the Irgun and Lechi] are traitors! … The Jewish Agency proposes herewith that all persons who are acquainted with any of the terrorists, should immediately inform the police…”
The decision was far from unanimous. Two members of the Jewish Agency resigned.
Thus began the Saison, or the hunting season, when the Haganah captured Irgun members, at times tortured them, and turned them over to the British authorities. Between November 1944 and March 1945, the names of close to a thousand Irgun members were passed on to the British. They were arrested, placed in detention camps, and some deported to Africa.
Palestine Police Force wanted poster of Irgun and Lehi members. Begin appears at the top left.
From his hideout, Begin condemned the Jewish Agency’s collaboration with the British. Yet, insisting, “There shall not be a war of brothers8,” he instructed the Irgun members not to take any action against the Jewish Agency or the Haganah.
The conflict only grew after the Holocaust, as Jewish refugees stranded in DP camps attempted to reach the Land of Israel and as the frustrated Irgun perpetrated more attacks on the British authorities.
Eventually, the Irgun won. Historians believe that it was due to their armed resistance that, in February 1947, the British announced the end of the Mandate and their withdrawal from Palestine9. The British Mandate officially terminated on May 14th, 1948, and Ben-Gurion proclaimed Israel’s independence, celebrated by the Jews and greatly opposed by the Arabs. Attacked by the neighboring Arab nations, the newborn State of Israel was plunged into the War of Independence.
Menachem Begin inspecting Irgun members in 1948. Public domain
The story of the Altalena began long before the British withdrawal. An American Revisionist Zionist organization that had attempted to rescue European Jewry throughout the Holocaust turned its attention to the plight of survivors. In 1947, they purchased a military ship that had participated in the D-Day invasion. The organization renamed the ship Altalena, after Jabotinsky’s pen name, and hired a mostly Jewish crew to operate it. The ship was intended to transport Jewish refugees, as well as weapons to assist the Irgun in its armed struggle against the British.
To accomplish such a feat under the nose of the British, the organizers collaborated with the French government, which was only too happy to help the Jews get rid of the British in the Middle East, thus increasing their own influence in the region. The French even provided the Jewish representatives with arms, in return for a promise of “significant freedom of action” in the Middle East10.
The Altalena on its way to Israel. Photo: Israel State Archives
At the same time, the Irgun coordinated the operation with the Jewish Agency. Though still suspicious of each other, the organizations agreed to work together on this common cause.
However, the negotiations and preparations took time. The Altalena finally sailed from France on June 11, 1948, weeks after the Declaration of Independence. On board were close to a thousand Jewish refugees, as well as a significant amount of guns, grenades, and ammunition.
Though there was no longer a need to smuggle the refugees clandestinely, the State of Israel, under attack by five Arab countries, remained in great need of weapons. Thus, when Begin informed Ben-Gurion about the Altalena, Ben-Gurion welcomed the news.
But there was a complication. Soon after the ship’s departure, the United Nations declared a two-week ceasefire between Israel and the Arab nations. It was an open secret that the Arabs were using the ceasefire to obtain more weapons. Thus, the provisional Israeli government did not object to the Altalena’s arrival in principle but instructed Begin to act carefully, out of the view of the U.N. observers. Under the circumstances, Begin decided to postpone the ship’s arrival.
However, communication with Altalena could not be established, and Begin’s instructions to wait were not received. Meanwhile, certain leaders of the Haganah became suspicious of the arms being brought into the country by the Irgun. Officially, the Israeli government authorized Altalena’s landing at Kfar Vitkin, near Netanya.
Crew members of the Altalena. Jabotinsky Archives, Tel Aviv, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
Even after the Declaration of Independence, the relations between the Haganah and the Irgun remained tense. The Haganah was now transformed into the Israel Defense Forces (IDF), the official army of the State of Israel. Ben-Gurion insisted that all the independent Jewish militias, such as the Irgun and Lechi, be incorporated into the army.
Begin, now out of hiding, held negotiations with Ben-Gurion. The Irgun members resented the idea of serving under Haganah commanders. As Begin acknowledged11, “It was not an easy matter to send our comrades to an army whose officers had hated the underground, persecuted it, besmirched it, kidnapped its members and handed over its officers… The men who were about to take command of our members had been systematically trained to hate them.”
Begin proposed a compromise. The Irgun members would form distinct units within the IDF, maintaining internal control over their own weapons. Ben-Gurion refused, insisting that the state could have only one army, with a unifying command structure.
In the beginning of June, Begin and Ben-Gurion finally signed an agreement stipulating the disbandment of the Irgun and its absorption into the IDF. However, the agreement would be in force “within the State of Israel12.” At the time, Jerusalem was excluded from the officially recognized State of Israel. Ben-Gurion and his colleagues had given up on it. To the Irgun, however, Jerusalem was an inseparable part of the Land of Israel. Some Irgun fighters remained in Jerusalem, still hoping to liberate it from the Jordanian invaders. They were running dangerously low on ammunition.
To Begin and his Irgun colleagues, it was implicit in the agreement that they would continue to fight for Jerusalem. Therefore, he requested that 20% of the ammunition arriving on Altalena be transferred to the Irgun members. To Begin, the request was perfectly reasonable, as it was the Irgun supporters who purchased the weapons, and he was willing to pass along 80% of them to the IDF. Ben-Gurion, however, insisted that all of the arriving weapons be under IDF’s jurisdiction.
It is unclear what exactly took place in the days before Altalena’s arrival. The key players have given contradictory testimonies in the ensuing decades about the conversations between the Israeli government and the Irgun leaders. Clearly, there was much miscommunication, fueled by years of distrust and hostility.
When Altalena approached Kfar Vitkin, its passengers and crew expected a warm welcome.
Ben-Gurion, however, remained extremely suspicious. When Israel Galili, the deputy minister of defense who had met with Begin, reported to Ben-Gurion that “a new and dangerous situation has arisen: a demand for a kind of private army, with private weapons13,” Ben-Gurion responded that this was unacceptable.
Shortly before Altalena’s landing at Kfar Vitkin, Ben-Gurion called an emergency session of the Cabinet. The Cabinet members expressed panic. Foreign Minister Moshe Shertok said, “We may now be facing a blatant, public violation of the truce by Jews14.” Ben-Gurion stated, “There are not going to be two armies. And Mr. Begin will not do whatever he feels like… If he does not give in, we shall open fire15.”
At 9 p.m. on June 20th, the Altalena stopped near the Kfar Vitkin beach. Begin came by motorboat to greet the new arrivals, amid much celebration. Within two hours, the passengers disembarked, and the unloading of the weapons began. Several dozen Irgun members gathered to help.
When IDF soldiers began surrounding the landing area, Begin remained unconcerned, convinced that an agreement with the government would be reached momentarily.
In the morning, the Government Press office issued an announcement16:
The Government regards this attempt by an independent group to bring in arms, particularly during the truce period, as a grave violation of Israel’s laws and of her international obligations, as well as an infringement on the clear agreement reached recently by the heads of [the Irgun, who] were to accept the authority of the state.
The Government regards this attempt by an independent group to bring in arms, particularly during the truce period, as a grave violation of Israel’s laws and of her international obligations, as well as an infringement on the clear agreement reached recently by the heads of [the Irgun, who] were to accept the authority of the state.
Begin was presented with an ultimatum demanding to relinquish all the weapons aboard Altalena within 10 minutes. Those on board were taken by surprise. Begin refused to believe that Ben-Gurion would follow through on his threats.
Meanwhile, the Israeli government began giving orders. When military pilots on a nearby base were ordered to bomb the Altalena, they refused. Boris Senior, a World War II veteran, said, “I will never be capable of bombing my Jewish brothers17.” Ben-Gurion had no choice but to abort the mission. Instead, he ordered the soldiers already at the beach to open fire. Though some IDF soldiers refused to shoot, others obeyed orders.
Despite the bullets flying around them, Begin and his second-in-command, Yaacov Meridor, ordered their men not to return fire. An Irgun fighter recalled18, “I couldn’t shoot. My brother was on the other side.” Another Irgun member recalled19, “We were confused and ashamed at the same time. Instead of welcoming us, they were killing and wounding many of our men whose only purpose was to help.”
Six Irgun men and two IDF soldiers were killed at Kfar Vitkin that day.
Altalena burning off the coast of Tel Aviv. Hans Pinn, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
Begin and other Irgun commanders boarded the Altalena and instructed the captain to head to Tel Aviv. Still hoping to resolve the tragic misunderstanding, Begin thought that proximity to Tel Aviv would gain them direct access to the government, as well as public support.
Shortly after midnight on June 21st, the Altalena ran aground 150 meters from the Tel Aviv beach. Several activists, including local mayors, tried to intervene and negotiate between the government and the Irgun, but Ben-Gurion insisted that the future of the State of Israel was at stake.
The Cabinet members later recalled Ben-Gurion, pacing nervously, stating that the only way to prevent a civil war was to destroy the munitions on the Altalena. In a 7-2 vote, the Cabinet decided to demand the ship’s unconditional surrender to the state.
When IDF officer Yitzchak Rabin arrived at the headquarters in the morning, he was informed that an insurrection was underway. Rabin recalled20, “Rumor follows rumor. [The Irgun] wants to take over all of Tel Aviv… no, even that is not enough… it intends to forcibly take control of the new state.”
Soldiers and civilians looking on as the Altalena burns off the coast of Tel Aviv. Photo: GPO
Rabin himself threw grenades at the Irgun members. Though many IDF soldiers refused to follow their orders, others complied and fired. Two Altalena crew members were killed and others wounded. Still, Irgun members did not return fire. Over the loudspeaker, they announced, “We want to negotiate… We don’t want to have war with our brothers.” But Ben-Gurion insisted on unconditional surrender.
At 4 p.m., Ben-Gurion ordered the artillery to fire at Altalena. The first three shots missed, but the fourth cannon shell hit Altalena’s hold and ignited a fire. The captain ordered everyone on board to abandon ship.
Eyewitnesses recall that even after the white flag was raised on the Altalena, the soldiers continued to shoot at the people evacuating the ship. The Irgun members suspected that Begin was the target. Begin himself was one of the last people to leave the ship. Throughout the ordeal, he urged his people not to return fire.
That day, ten men from the Altalena and one IDF soldier lost their lives.
After the Altalena incident, Ben-Gurion remained convinced that he had done the right thing. Begin, on the other hand, was heartbroken. The next day, he delivered a tearful radio address. After refuting the rumors of armed rebellion, Begin reminded his listeners21, “Do not raise a hand against a brother, not even today!”
Later in life, Begin wrote that he wanted to be remembered, “above all, as someone who prevented civil war.22” Even after serving as the sixth prime minister of the State of Israel, he considered his refusal to open fire during the Altalena affair his greatest accomplishment.
A year after the affair, Ben-Gurion ordered the burned-out hull of the Altalena towed out and sunk into the sea. For decades, its exact location remained unknown.
On August 24th, 2026, the Israeli Heritage Ministry in conjunction with National Security Minister announced that the Altalena has been located about 20 kilometers off the coast of Israel, at a depth of 503 meters. After years of searching, the discovery was made using advanced sensors and other technology.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu congratulated everyone involved. In an official statement, he said23:
[T]his is an emotional, foundational moment. Off the coast of Tel Aviv, the Altalena went up in flames; … brothers fell by the hands of brothers. But precisely out of the infernal fire, burst forth the immortal cry of the commander of the Etzel, Menachem Begin of blessed memory, to stop the firing that was taking place… because we will not go to a civil war. This is the great lesson of the Altalena. It is as true today as it was true then. Because division is weakness, and unity is strength.

But precisely out of the infernal fire, burst forth the immortal cry of the commander of the Etzel, Menachem Begin of blessed memory, to stop the firing that was taking place… because we will not go to a civil war. This is the great lesson of the Altalena. It is as true today as it was true then. Because division is weakness, and unity is strength.

If this channel is truly about wisdom, purpose, and seeking a more enlightened life, then difficult questions should be examined from every angle. In 1982, 22-year-old tank soldier Yehuda Katz disappeared during the Battle of Sultan Yacoub in Lebanon’s Bekaa Valley. His armored battalion had driven into a Syrian ambush and fought desperately through the night. The battle claimed the lives of 21 Israeli soldiers. Yehuda was among those declared missing.
For 44 years, his fate remained unknown. At what point do you allow yourself to give up hope?
In August 2026, the IDF and Mossad announced they’d recovered Yehuda’s remains in a covert operation. He was brought home and buried on Jerusalem’s Mount of Olives.
From left to left: Zechariah Baumel, Zvi Feldman, Yehuda Katz
At the shiva, I spoke with his brother Avi and his sister Perachia.
“This is an unusual shiva,” I said. “This this comes after 44 years of waiting. Surely you mourned Yehuda’s death long ago.”
“We never mourned him,” they said. “We never gave up hope that at any moment Yehuda might walk through the door.”
Every Friday night before Kiddush, the family recited a special prayer that Yehuda will return this week. When going away, they’d leave a note: “Yehuda, if you come while we’re away, welcome home! Here’s where we’re staying. There’s plenty of food in the refrigerator...”
For 44 years, the Katz family held on with stubborn, audacious hope.
In 1985, three years after the fateful battle, Hezi Shai, one of the soldiers captured with Yehuda and presumed dead, was freed from captivity. His story strengthened the possibility that Yehuda could also return alive.
Their hope was further kindled when Shai reported hearing the terrorists speak about Yehuda in a way that suggested he was alive.
As long as the question of Yehuda’s fate remained open, the Katz family refused to close the door.
As long as the question of Yehuda’s fate remained open, the Katz family refused to close the door.
On another occasion, the IDF received four coffins purportedly containing the remains of captive Israeli soldiers. Upon examination, only one coffin contained the remains of a Jewish soldier; the other three bodies were Arab.
As long as the question of Yehuda’s fate remained open, the Katz family refused to close the door.
The Katz family felt that surrendering hope would mean abandoning Yehuda – who might still be waiting for them.
Imagine someone returning after decades in captivity, only to discover that everyone had moved on. “Why did you give up on me?”
The Katz family did not suspend their lives or pretend that everything was fine. Yet they would not declare the story over before the last chapter is written.
Yehuda himself embodied that same loyalty. A brilliant yet humble Torah scholar, he assisted Rabbi Chaim Yaakov Goldvicht, head of Yeshivat Kerem B’Yavneh, in preparing his central weekly lecture.
Yehuda’s sharp mind was matched by an extraordinary heart. At age nine, upon learning that a younger child in school had lost a parent, he appointed himself the boy’s “big brother,” watching over him and ensuring that he was never excluded.
Already at a young age, Yehuda understood: No one should be left alone.
When Hezi Shai, the captive later freed, was imprisoned in Syria, he sustained himself with the conviction that his country would do everything to bring him home. Every day he imagined an Entebbe-style rescue with Israeli soldiers suddenly break through the floor of his cell.
This commitment demoralizes Israel’s enemies. They see how tenaciously Israel fights for every soldier and hostage, how much they are willing to sacrifice, and how deeply that commitment unites the nation.
For 44 years, Yehuda’s family refused to mourn him while any possibility remained that he was alive. Yehuda’s parents, Sarah and Yosef, unfortunately did not live to see him brought home.
But now, the circle of Sultan Yacoub has finally closed, with Yehuda returned to the soil of the land he loved.
“There is hope for your future,” God tells Rachel. “Your children shall return to their own border” (Jeremiah 31:16).
Yehuda’s sister told me: “God gave us with the strength until now. And God will give us the strength going forward.”
May the nation's courage and dedication to its brave defenders always match that of this heroic family. May the memory of this fallen warrior always be a blessing. Am Yisreal Chai.
answers.author: Rabbi Shraga Simmons

questions.title: How to Become More Emotionally Connected to Yourself, Your Spouse, and God
questions.question: How to Become More Emotionally Connected to Yourself, Your Spouse, and God

answers.text:
Simple ways to feel closer to your spouse, yourself, and God this Elul, no big gestures required.
Have you ever been in a room full of people yet felt alone? Or sat next to your spouse yet felt miles apart? Or stood in synagogue, saying words you've said year after year, wondering, Does God even hear me?
Loneliness isn’t the absence of people; it's the absence of emotional connection. It's commonly felt in marriage, within yourself, and in your relationship with God.
We give energy to our jobs, children, communities – even our phones. Then at 10:30pm we turn to our spouse and ask, "Okay, what do you need?" Our prime time should be given to our spouse, not our leftover energy.
Preserve energy for your spouse by saying no to others during the day, delegating tasks, or decreasing expectations of yourself. (Aka dinner can be plain rice and simple chicken, nothing fancy.)
Then, when you’re actually in front of your spouse, make a conscious choice to put down the phone and give them a few minutes of undivided attention. Don't just ask them how their day was -- go a drop deeper. Ask them the hardest part of their day, the best part of their day, or what's been weighing on their mind lately. When they answer, don't jump to fix it; just listen, validate, or offer a hug.
Your spouse wants your physical presence and needs your emotional energy as well.
You can become a stranger to yourself. You know you need sleep but you keep going. You need friendship but you're too busy to call. You need quiet but you immediately reach for your phone.
You distract yourself, overeat, or scroll, anything to avoid sitting quietly enough to hear what's happening inside.
How am I actually doing? What am I pretending doesn't bother me? What part of myself have I silenced because I'm afraid of disappointing someone?
Emotionally disconnecting from the self includes denying yourself things that make you feel alive. Make sure to listen to your inner voice and fill your bucket.
Give yourself five minutes of true quiet each day -- no phone, no music, just you. Notice what surfaces when you stop filling the silence.
Do one thing because it makes you feel alive, not because it's productive or expected of you. A walk, a hobby, a few pages of a book.
There have been times I've rushed through prayers so quickly I literally swallow my words. And then I finish and think: What just happened?
I prayed, but where was the connection? The Hebrew month of Elul is an opportune time to bring God into your daily life.
Make prayer personal. Use your own language and wording to tell God what you're worried about, grateful for, struggling with, and hoping for, as if you're speaking to someone who truly knows you.
Look for the small moments of Divine providence. Recognize that serendipity is God's guiding hand in your life. Recognize the small moments of kindness, beauty, and blessing. The more we notice, the more connected you feel.
One minute of gratitude, filling in a gratitude journal, or a heartfelt "Thank You" to God for help, can turn an ordinary moment into a relationship. Even one small step in the right direction can bring change and connection.
The month of Elul gives you a beautiful opportunity to rebuild your connection with your spouse, with yourself, and with God.
Perhaps that is why Judaism gives us three central practices for this time of year: teshuvah (repentance), tefillah (prayer), and tzedakah (charity).
Teshuvah reconnects you to yourself. It asks us to stop, look inward, and honestly consider who you have become and who you want to be. It’s a recalibration to get recentered with your soul, your true inner self.
Prayer reconnects you to God. It reminds you that you are never truly alone -- and that you can turn to Him with your worries, gratitude, hopes, and questions, any time, day or night.
Tzedakah reconnects you to others. It moves you beyond yourself by reminding you that you are part of something larger than your own life.
This Elul, take one small step towards strengthening your most important relationships, with your spouse, with yourself, and with God.
Join Sarah Pachter for an honest, heart-to-heart conversation about the quiet disconnect so many women feel in their marriages, and how to find real intimacy and being truly seen by the person closest to you. Wednesday, September 9, 12:00pm EST. Free. Register now: https://events.jewishworkshops.com/youbelonghere
answers.author: Sarah Pachter

questions.title: Samson – Contact with Dead
questions.question: I’m trying to understand something. Shimshon (Samson) was a nazir (Nazarite), which is why he didn’t cut his hair or drink wine. But isn’t one of the restrictions of a Nazarite not to come in contact with the dead (Numbers 6:6-7)? How was he able to fight wars and kill Philistines, as well as slay a lion and take the jawbone of a donkey?

answers.text:
It's a very good question. The Talmud explains that Samson was a unique type of Nazarite. Since he didn't make the vow himself but it was decreed upon him from heaven before his birth, he was only a Nazarite for those things the angel specified to his parents – namely cutting his hair and consuming products of the vine (Judges 13:4-5). Samson was thus permitted to come in contact with dead bodies. (In fact, the Talmud likewise states anyone who accepts upon himself to be “a Nazarite as Samson” likewise becomes this unique type of Nazarite.)
(In terms of coming in contact with dead animals, that is not an issue for any type of Nazarite. The Torah only forbids his coming in contact with “a dead soul” – but not a dead animal (which doesn’t possess a true soul) (Talmud Nazir 48a).)
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: Adam’s Sin and the Decree of Death
questions.question: The Torah states that on the day Adam would eat of the fruit of the Tree of Knowledge he would surely die (Genesis 2:17). Yet although he was punished when he sinned, he didn’t die on that day, but lived hundreds of years longer. Am I missing something?

answers.text:
It’s an excellent question. There are several answers to this, most of which are variations of a single theme. To explain, we need to first have a deeper understanding of Adam’s sin.
Before Adam and Eve ate of the Tree of Knowledge, they were both spiritually and physically perfect. Man had no Evil Inclination. He had no inner desire for evil. The drive for evil was an external force, embodied in the Serpent, which attempted to lure man to sin. But man himself was wholly pure. His physical side was nothing other than a perfect reflection of his spirit.
As a result, before the Sin, man had the potential to live forever. His body did not contain the decaying influence of the Evil Inclination. His physical side had the same potential as his soul to be wholly perfected and to exist eternally. As the Kabbalists explain, had Adam and Eve passed their test and not eaten of the Tree of Knowledge, they would have afterwards eaten of the Tree of Life – to live eternally with God in Eden.
Once man sinned, however, evil became a part of his psyche. The Tree of Knowledge gave him an intimate knowledge of – and desire for – evil. Man’s evil inclination was no longer an external Serpent, but a part of his very soul. Man became a confused mixture of good and evil, the good only attaining ascendancy after the utmost of struggles. And man would never be fully secure in his spirituality. As high as his soul might strive upwards, his body would drag him down. He would never be entirely free of his physical wants and desirous nature.
As a result, death was a necessary part of man’s existence. Man could now never entirely perfect himself. His body was simply too corrupt for full rectification. It would have to die and decay – only to later be recreated in a higher state at the Resurrection, at which point – if it is worthy – to live forever (Derech Hashem I 3:9).
Based on the above, many of the commentators to the Torah explain that the punishment of death decreed on man did not mean to say Adam would literally die right then, but at that point he would be liable to death (Targum Yonatan, Ramban, Rabbeinu Bechaye, Chizkuni, Radak and many others), or that because of his imperfections death would now slowly overtake him (Malbim, also brought in Ibn Ezra 3:8).
